newsitem.title: USA: RESEARCH ALERT-Settlement could aid tobacco stocks.
newsitem.headline: RESEARCH ALERT-Settlement could aid tobacco stocks.

text.p: Tobacco stock prices would soar as much as 20 to 25 percent if the industry agreed to enter an industrywide settlement, Sanford C. Bernstein analyst Gary Black said in a research report.

Black said he expects the industry to agree to be regulated by the government and to pay into a settlement fund in exchange for a deal that protects the companies from any future claims for injuries caused by tobacco.
"We believe the settlement debate will only intensify in the coming months," Black said in the report.
Black made his comments at the end of a week in which the chief executive of U.K. tobacco giant B.A.T Industries Plc said his company would consider a settlement.
The comments on British television by Martin Broughton, B.A.T's chief executive, marked the second time a leading tobacco executive implied a settlement was not out of the question.
Steven Goldstone, RJR Nabsico Holdings Corp's chief executive, has also expressed a willingness to consider the issue.

The week also held an industry seminar that was a rare open forum for Wall Street and institutional investors to carefully examine the future fiscal safety of tobacco holdings, which is something most of the financial community has been reluctant to face.

Black reiterated his outperform ratings on both Philip Morris Cos Inc and RJR Nabisco. He targets a price of $140 per share for Philip Morris "over the next few months," while keeping his price target for RJR Nabisco at $40.
"We would be inclined to increase both target prices if we obtained additional evidence that a legislative deal was imminent," Black said.
Philip Morris stock was down 3/8 at 124-3/4 in Friday afternoon trading at the New York Stock Exchange, while RJR Nabisco was up 1/4 at 35-1/4.
He said noted the industry's "clear shift in strategy toward settlement over the past 12 months," and attributed it to:
-- the industry's first loss in a personal injury case last summer;

-- the industry's "clearly deteriorating legal position in the Florida Medicaid case," due for an August trial. He noted the judge's refusal to allow defense tactics traditionally employed by tobacco companies and said the industry stands a 50-50 chance of losing the case.
-- the likelihood that politics in Washington, with a Republican-controlled Congress for the next two years, presented the best opportunity to achieve a favorable settlement.

"The doomsday crowd continues to miss one fundamental point about tobacco: Unlike other products involved in mass torts, cigarettes will continue to be sold even if hundreds of juries declare them to be dangerous," Black said.
